How 'Sangeetha' Nearly Destroyed a Thirty-Seven-Year Marriage

# How 'Sangeetha' Nearly Destroyed a Thirty-Seven-Year Marriage

### Or, Why Every Retired Software Architect Eventually Ends Up at Narada Gana Sabha

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

![Amaruvi Devanathan's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Bq_i!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F357700fd-8e69-44fa-a5f8-000e6e26808a_1002x1002.jpeg)

Retirement is a strange concept.

Particularly for 58+ age group software professionals from Chennai.

Sundaram, 61, fondly called Server Sundaram by peers, Sundaram Sir by juniors and Sundaram mama by Gen Z in Mylapore, used to be an expert on Mainframe Servers and hence the prefix ‘Server’. ( No connection to the Nagesh starrer ).

For nearly four decades, Sundaram Mama was treated like a minor deity in the corporate ecosystem.

Meetings were scheduled around his availability.

Junior developers feared his code reviews.

Managers quoted his opinions as though they were constitutional amendments.

Clients in New Jersey attended calls at impossible hours because Sundaram Mama had said, “Let’s quickly sync.”

Nothing about those calls was ever quick.

Yet people attended.

Such was his power.

Then one Friday afternoon the company organized a farewell.

There was a cake large enough to feed an entire project team.

There was a plaque nobody would dust.

There was a speech containing the phrase “valuable contribution” seven times.

There were photographs.

Handshakes.

LinkedIn recommendations. ( Don’t ask why Linkedin recommendation for a 60 year old retired software person).

A standing ovation from people already checking their emails.

By evening his laptop stopped working.

By next morning his access card no longer opened the gate.

For thirty-eight years people had called him before making decisions.

Now even the coffee machine no longer recognized him.

Retirement is the only promotion where everybody celebrates you on Friday and forgets you by Monday.

Sundaram Mama discovered this with alarming speed.

His retirement itself lasted exactly four days.

By Day Five he had identified a serious problem.

The production environment at home was unstable.

The root cause was Savitri Mami.

Specifically her breakfast roadmap.

Now, fairness demands that we pause here.

Savitri Mami had been cooking for forty years.

Thousands of breakfasts.

Thousands of lunches.

Thousands of dinners.

Entire generations had been educated, employed and married on the strength of her cooking.

For most of their married life, Sundaram Mama had simply eaten whatever appeared on the plate and rushed to office.

He never conducted reviews.

He never submitted feedback.

He never organized stakeholder meetings regarding chutney consistency.

Then retirement happened.

And suddenly he had time.

Time to observe.

Time to compare.

Time to benchmark.

Time to produce performance evaluations for breakfast.

No marriage is designed to survive that much free time.

Every morning at exactly 7:30, Savitri Mami produced Rava Upma.

Not ordinary upma.

Architectural upma.

Enterprise-grade upma.

Monolithic upma.

Upma so structurally sound that civil engineers could use it as a reference material.

Road contractors could repair potholes with it. BTW, Mylapore’s roads needed that.

NASA could potentially test heat shields against it.

One morning Sundaram poked it gently. Just once.

The spoon bounced.

The plate vibrated.

A nearby tumbler shifted position.

“Savi,” he said carefully, the shorter form for that already short name ‘Savitri’.

“Enna?”

“This is not breakfast.”

“What is it then?”

“This is technical debt.”

She stared.

“What?”

“For thirty years this upma has accumulated unresolved issues.”

“You eat.”

“I am trying.”

“It is healthy.”

“So is reinforced concrete.”

The coffee wasn’t helping.

To be fair, Savitri’s coffee looked exactly like coffee.

It smelled approximately like coffee.

But somewhere between decoction and execution, a runtime error had occurred.

Every sip felt like debugging legacy COBOL code written by somebody who retired before the Emergency.

Somehow R.K.Narayan’s lines emerged in Sundaram’s amygdala. “He pushed two idlis into his mouth and washed it down with a tumbler of coffee”. Probably Narayan’s wife made drinkable coffee, thought Sundaram, without opening his mouth.

By the second week of retirement, Sundaram had developed a daily escape protocol.

At precisely 8:17 a.m. he would announce:

“Small walk.”

The phrase “small walk” has many meanings in Mylapore.

It can mean exercise.

It can mean temple visit.

It can mean gossip.

It can mean avoiding relatives.

It can mean pretending to buy coriander while spending ninety minutes discussing geopolitics.

In Sundaram’s case it meant:

**Mission Escape Upma.**

Destination:

Narada Gana Sabha.

More specifically:

The legendary Sangeetha canteen.

Among retired Mylapore men, this establishment occupied a status somewhere between Tirupati and Switzerland.

People spoke about it with religious sincerity.

“Have you tried the jasmine idli?”

“Besh besh.”

“The Kasi halwa?”

“Pramaadham.”

“The coffee?”

“Direct moksham.”

Every morning retired men migrated there in organized formations.

Some carried newspapers.

Some carried walking sticks.

Most carried opinions.

Many carried all three.

The canteen was not merely a restaurant.

It was an unofficial rehabilitation centre for retired husbands.

Nobody admitted this openly.

Officially they came for breakfast.

Unofficially they came because somebody still remembered their usual order.

At home they were retired.

Here they were regulars.

The difference mattered.

On a particularly glorious morning, Sundaram Mama occupied his usual seat.

A plate of idlis arrived.

These were not idlis.

These were engineering achievements - not even a properly written Business Requirement Document could produce, thought Sundaram.

Soft enough to awaken childhood memories.

Light enough to qualify as cloud infrastructure.

A strong breeze could probably migrate them to another district.

He stared reverentially.

“Look at this.”

His friend Krishnamurthy arrived.

Retired Vice President of Enterprise Platforms.

Specialist in unsolicited advice.

“What happened?”

“Observe the architecture.”

Krishnamurthy examined the idli.

“Excellent load balancing.”

“Exactly.”

“Texture distribution is optimal.”

“Correct.”

“World-class porosity.”

“Absolutely.”

Both nodded solemnly.

Nearby customers assumed they were discussing semiconductor manufacturing.

The conversation naturally shifted toward coffee.

Every conversation in Mylapore eventually becomes a coffee conversation.

Discussions about politics become coffee discussions.

Discussions about cricket become coffee discussions.

Even discussions about international conflict somehow ended with somebody saying, “But have you tried the degree coffee at...”

Krishnamurthy took a sip.

Closed his eyes.

“Perfect.”

Sundaram nodded.

“Good degree coffee is exactly like microservice architecture.”

“Explain.”

“The decoction must be independent.”

“Correct.”

“The milk must scale horizontally.”

“Naturally.”

“The sugar integration must be seamless.”

“Obviously.”

“No single component should dominate.”

“Precisely.”

“If milk dominates?”

“Monolith.”

“If sugar dominates?”

“System override.”

“If decoction is weak?”

“Service outage.”

“And if all three work together?”

“Moksha.”

They clinked tumblers, and said “Attahaasam” in unison, like they cheer the company CEO during any Town Hall.

A nearby engineering student quietly started taking notes.

The food kept arriving.

Mini pongal.

Karamani sundal.

Vadai.

Kasi halwa.

Each item received a detailed technical review.

Then came the ghee roast.

Sundaram leaned back.

“Ghee Roast Crispness Index.”

“What is today’s score?”

“Nine point four.”

“Out of ten?”

“Out of existence.”

The table approved.

Meanwhile conversation drifted toward politics.

Which is always dangerous in Mylapore.

Within six minutes somebody references Rajaji.

Within ten minutes somebody quotes the Mahabharata.

Within fifteen minutes somebody blames television anchors.

The topic that morning was the astonishing rise of the Vijay Government.

Nobody had fully recovered from it.

Krishnamurthy shook his head.

“I still cannot believe it.”

Sundaram nodded.

“This government is exactly like thideer upma.”

The table erupted.

“Correct.”

“Unexpected.”

“Appeared suddenly.”

“Nobody remembers ordering it.”

Subscribe

Sundaram continued.

“Initially everybody is optimistic.”

“Because of the turmeric color?”

“Because optimism and turmeric look identical from a distance.”

Laughter exploded.

Krishnamurthy joined in.

“The first spoon is exciting.”

“The second spoon creates questions.”

“The third spoon creates analysis.”

“The fourth spoon requires antacid.”

One Mama adjusted his spectacles.

“Will it survive five years?”

Another shrugged.

“Depends on digestion.”

A third observed:

“Every government is basically a kitchen experiment, almost all have kitchen cabinet.”

“Some become sakkarai pongal.”

“Some become burnt rasam.”

“And some become thideer kichadi with a press conference.”

The table roared.

For retired men this was superior to Netflix.

Back home, however, disaster was quietly loading.

The source was WhatsApp.

As always.

No civilization has suffered more from WhatsApp than middle-aged Indians.

That afternoon Sundaram sent a message to Krishnamurthy.

It read:

**“Tomorrow morning I am meeting Sangeetha at Narada Gana Sabha. Her filter coffee brings me back to life.”**

A perfectly innocent message.

A message referring to a canteen.

Unfortunately fate enjoys entertainment.

Savitri Mami saw it.

Now, it must be said that Savitri Mami was not normally suspicious.

After thirty-seven years of marriage, suspicion requires stamina.

And stamina is a resource best conserved.

But there are certain words capable of awakening memories buried for decades.

One of them was “Sangeetha.”

Back in 1983, when engineering colleges still believed practical records should be handwritten and telephones required patience, there had allegedly been a girl named Sangeetha.

Not a romance.

Not a relationship.

Not even a conversation of consequence.

Merely admiration from a respectful distance of thirty-two feet.

Like appreciating a temple gopuram.

The matter had been forgotten.

By everyone.

Except Savitri Mami.

Wives possess archival capabilities that would make Google jealous.

Events from 1983 remain instantly retrievable.

The moment she saw the message, her imagination launched a full-scale deployment.

Within minutes she had created an entire storyline.

College crush returns.

Retired husband reconnects.

Secret meetings.

Coffee romance.

Senior citizen scandal.

Possibly accompanied by discount coupons.

She opened older chats.

More evidence.

“Sangeetha coffee.”

“Sangeetha pongal.”

“Sangeetha idli.”

“Sangeetha saved my life.” ( She read as “Sangeetha be my wife”).

The case was building itself.

That evening she watched him closely.

He hummed while reading the newspaper.

Suspicious.

He ironed a shirt.

Very suspicious.

He polished sandals.

Practically a confession.

The next morning Sundaram prepared for departure.

Fresh veshti.

Fresh vibuthi.

Mild happiness.

The innocence of a man heading toward pongal.

Behind him, Savitri prepared for battle.

At 9:15 a.m. she entered Narada Gana Sabha with the velocity of a Tamil cinema heroine approaching the climax.

Her pace alone could have improved Chennai traffic management, but for the metro works that would end in 2047 when India becomes ‘Visit Bharat’.

She scanned the canteen.

Where was Sangeetha?

Where was this woman?

Where was the destroyer of breakfasts?

Then she saw him.

Sundaram Mama.

Seated peacefully.

Utterly oblivious.

In front of him sat not a glamorous college sweetheart.

Not a mysterious woman.

Not a yoga instructor.

Not even another 60 year old lady.

Instead there was a mountain of Ghee Podi Kozhukattai.

He was attacking it with focus normally reserved for production outages.

One hand held a spoon.

The other protected the plate from competitors.

A tumbler of coffee stood nearby like a loyal security guard, the one ‘guarding’ Vai.Ko., the politician who is the leader of a party that has no members.

Savitri stopped.

Blink.

Blink again.

No Sangeetha.

Only food. More food. Then even more food.

At precisely that moment the waiter arrived.

“Sir, one more coffee from your Sangeetha?”

Sundaram smiled.

“Definitely.”

The waiter disappeared toward the kitchen.

The truth arrived.

Not woman.

Restaurant.

For three full seconds Savitri considered her options.

Return home quietly?

Impossible.

Pretend this was accidental?

Unconvincing.

Launch attack?

Most practical.

She marched forward.

“Sundaram!”

The entire table froze.

Every retired man immediately became interested.

Free entertainment.

Sundaram looked up.

“Saaavi? What a surprise.” - the extra ‘aa’ signifying surprise, as English doesn't have the supporting letter to increase the elongation of a letter, unlike other Indian languages.

“What is happening here?”

He looked around.

“Breakfast.”

“What about Sangeetha?”

He pointed toward the kitchen.

“There.”

Silence.

Krishnamurthy understood instantly.

His shoulders began shaking.

Then came laughter.

Then uncontrollable laughter.

Soon three tables were laughing.

One man nearly inhaled a vadai.

Savitri finally understood.

Her face turned the color of tomato chutney.

Sundaram’s expression moved from confusion to enlightenment.

Then he committed a fatal error.

He laughed.

Never laugh immediately.

It violates all known marriage protocols.

The entire canteen fell silent.

Even the ceiling fans appeared nervous.

Then something remarkable happened.

The waiter arrived carrying coffee.

“Madam, please sit.”

A tumbler appeared.

Then mini tiffin.

Then sweet.

The canteen had witnessed decades of marriages.

It understood conflict resolution better than most counsellors.

Feed everybody.

Within ten minutes both were eating.

Within twenty minutes both were arguing about coffee.

Within thirty minutes normal operations resumed.

Savitri reluctantly admitted the coffee was excellent.

Sundaram reluctantly admitted that her coffee possessed “certain strengths.”

This diplomatic statement was accepted.

Krishnamurthy later described it as the most successful marital hotfix of the decade.

Today the routine continues.

Every morning Sundaram still announces:

“Small walk.”

Every morning Savitri rolls her eyes.

Sometimes she joins him.

Sometimes she does not.

Sometimes they sit opposite each other sharing pongal, coffee and opinions about governments they never voted for.

Sometimes they argue.

Sometimes they laugh.

Sometimes they simply sit quietly.

After thirty-seven years of marriage, silence is also a language.

Young people think this story is about food.

It is not.

The food is only infrastructure.

The coffee is merely middleware.

The real service running underneath is companionship.

Retirement takes away titles.

It takes away meetings.

It takes away deadlines.

It takes away the comforting illusion that the world cannot function without you.

What remains is a wife who still remembers things you forgot.

A steel tumbler of coffee.

A familiar canteen.

A few friends who laugh at the same jokes for the hundredth time.

And perhaps that is the secret genius of Mylapore.

Not the sabhas.

Not the concerts.

Not even the food.

It is the fact that an entire civilization has learned how to convert domestic bugs into public entertainment, yet pretend innocence.

Elsewhere people attend therapy.

In Mylapore they attend canteens.

Elsewhere people discuss emotional compatibility.

In Mylapore they discuss ghee roast crispness indexes.

Elsewhere political revolutions reshape society.

In Mylapore they are compared to thideer upma and judged accordingly.

So if you ever overhear a retired Mylapore gentleman saying:

“I am meeting Sangeetha. Her coffee gives me life.”

Do not panic.

Do not activate family WhatsApp groups.

Do not summon relatives.

Do not initiate forensic investigations.

Most likely he is not pursuing romance. Even he does, it would be a one way traffic.

He is pursuing breakfast.

And frankly, after surviving thirty-eight years of corporate meetings, production outages, spaghetti code, cloud migrations, impossible deadlines, repetitive juvenile Town Halls, performance reviews, and homemade upma capable of supporting highway construction, the man has earned it.

Besh. Besh.

Let him drink his coffee in peace.

Because every Chennaiite knows the truth.

The most stable love triangle in Mylapore is not husband-wife-other woman.

It is husband-wife-sabha canteen.
